title: Can Masturbation Become a False Comfort?
paragraphs:
Can Masturbation Become a False Comfort?
When the Thing That Soothes You Starts Quietly Owning You
There are nights when nobody knows.
The room is quiet.
The phone is close.
The loneliness is louder than usual.
Maybe you are not even thinking about sex at first.
Maybe you are thinking about rejection.
Stress.
A marriage that feels cold.
A relationship that ended.
A prayer that seems unanswered.
The pressure you carried all day.
The memories you wish you could erase.
Or simply that strange emptiness that settles over the soul when everyone else has gone to sleep.
And you want relief.
Not necessarily rebellion.
Not necessarily some dramatic declaration that you are walking away from God.
Just relief.
Something that will make the ache disappear for a few minutes.
And that is where this conversation becomes deeper than masturbation.
Because sometimes the most spiritually dangerous question is not merely:
“Is this sexual act sinful?”
Sometimes the deeper question is:
“What am I asking this behavior to do for my soul that I should be bringing to God?”
Stay with that question.
Because it may uncover something you have been fighting for years without understanding why you keep returning to it.
The Bible does not contain a verse that explicitly says, “You shall not masturbate.”
That needs to be stated clearly.
Christians should never pretend Scripture says something it does not say.

Genesis 38 is sometimes used as though Onan’s sin were simply masturbation, but the passage describes something different: Onan deliberately refused his covenantal responsibility to provide offspring for his deceased brother while exploiting the sexual relationship for himself. We should not force that passage to say more than it actually says.
But saying that Scripture never explicitly names masturbation does not mean Scripture has nothing meaningful to say about it.
The Bible speaks profoundly about sexual desire.
About lust.
About the imagination.
About self-control.
About enslavement.
About the body.
About secrecy.
About worship.
About comfort.
And ultimately about what happens when a human heart repeatedly runs somewhere other than God for salvation from its pain.
That is where the question becomes uncomfortable.
Can masturbation become a false comfort?
Yes.
Not because an orgasm possesses some mystical power that automatically separates a person from God.
But because almost anything can become spiritually disordered when we repeatedly ask it to give us what only God can ultimately provide.
Food can become comfort.
Alcohol can become comfort.
Work can become comfort.
Shopping can become comfort.
Entertainment can become comfort.
Attention can become comfort.
Pornography can become comfort.
Sex can become comfort.
And masturbation can become comfort too.
The issue is not merely what your hands are doing.
The issue may be where your heart is running.
Jesus repeatedly went beneath visible behavior and exposed the hidden movements of the heart.
In Matthew 5:28, He says:
“Everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart.”

The Greek expression translated “to lust after her” contains the verb ἐπιθυμέω — epithymeō, meaning to desire, long for, or covet. Desire itself is not automatically sinful; context determines its moral character. Here Christ is confronting sexual desire that deliberately turns another person into the object of covetous consumption.
Jesus takes holiness into places nobody else can see.
The imagination.
The intention.
The private gaze.
The secret appetite.

That matters enormously when discussing masturbation because, for many people, masturbation is intertwined with pornography, sexual fantasy, remembered images, imagined bodies, or the deliberate cultivation of lust.
At that point the Christian cannot honestly reduce the question to:
“Where does the Bible specifically mention masturbation?”
The more revealing question becomes:
“What am I feeding in my heart while I do it?”
And perhaps an even deeper one:
“Why do I need this right now?”
That question can hurt.
Because sometimes the answer is not:
“I am overwhelmed with sexual desire.”
Sometimes the answer is:
“I feel unwanted.”
“I feel anxious.”
“I am lonely.”
“I am angry.”
“I cannot sleep.”
“I hate myself tonight.”
“I had a terrible day.”
“My spouse rejected me.”
“I miss someone.”
“I feel numb.”
“I need something to make me feel good.”
“I don't want to think anymore.”
Suddenly the struggle looks different.
You thought you were fighting a sexual habit.
You may also have been trying to medicate a wounded heart.
And if that is true, shame alone will never heal you.
You can hate the behavior and still return to it because you have never addressed the wound underneath it.
This is one reason Paul's words in 1 Corinthians are so penetrating.
He writes:
The Greek phrase behind “I will not be dominated” uses ἐξουσιασθήσομαι — exousiasthēsomai, carrying the sense of being brought under another's authority or mastery.
That gives us an extraordinarily useful biblical question.
Not merely:
“Can I technically do this?”
But:
“Is this mastering me?”
Can you say no?
Can you experience loneliness without immediately needing sexual release?
Can you experience anxiety without reaching automatically for pornography or fantasy?
Can you lie awake uncomfortable without needing the familiar escape?
Can you feel rejection without soothing yourself sexually?
Can you go without it without becoming restless, irritable, preoccupied, or consumed?
Can you bring the urge before Christ rather than obeying it immediately?
Because there is a difference between experiencing desire and being ruled by desire.
Paul tells believers in 1 Corinthians 6:19–20 that their bodies are temples of the Holy Spirit and concludes:
“Therefore glorify God in your body.”
Think about the dignity contained in that sentence.
Your body is not garbage.
Your sexuality is not garbage.
Your sexual desire does not make you disgusting.
Christian holiness is not hatred of the human body.
Christianity makes the astonishing claim that the body matters so much that Christ redeemed the whole person and promises bodily resurrection.
Your body belongs to the Lord.
Which means the Christian question is not simply:
“How close can I get to sin without technically crossing the line?”
It becomes:
“How can this body glorify the One who purchased me with His blood?”
That changes everything.
Because now sexuality is no longer merely about release.
It becomes discipleship.
And discipleship includes learning that not every desire must immediately become an action.
Paul names ἐγκράτεια — enkrateia, self-control, among the fruit of the Spirit in Galatians 5:22–23.
Self-control is not pretending desire does not exist.
It is not becoming emotionally numb.
It is not despising sexuality.
It is the Spirit-produced freedom to experience a desire without becoming its servant.
There is tremendous freedom in realizing:
An urge is not a command.
You can feel something without obeying it.
You can experience temptation without surrendering to it.
You can experience loneliness without anesthetizing it.
You can experience sexual tension without believing you will collapse unless you release it immediately.
And sometimes the moment between desire and action becomes holy ground.
Because that is where you discover what actually owns you.
Maybe you have promised God a hundred times:
“Never again.”
Then three days later you fell.
Maybe three hours later.
Maybe twenty minutes later.
Then came the familiar disgust.
“How could I pray after doing that?”
“How could God still want me?”
“I promised Him.”
“I knew better.”
“I am filthy.”
“I am fake.”
“I should hide.”
And this is where another enemy enters the room.
Not merely lust.
Shame.
Shame tells you that because you fell, you should run away from the only Person who can restore you.
But watch what happens after humanity's first sin.
Adam tells God in Genesis 3:
“I was afraid... and I hid myself.”
Sin has been teaching human beings to hide ever since.
Hide the browser history.
Hide the fantasies.
Hide the habit.
Hide from your spouse.
Hide from your pastor.
Hide from your Christian friends.
And eventually...
hide from God.
But hiding does not heal what grace is inviting into the light.
The apostle John writes:
The Gospel does not say:
“Clean yourself thoroughly enough and perhaps Jesus will accept you again.”
The Gospel says something far more scandalous.
Christ came for sinners.
Real ones.
Secret ones.
Repeat offenders.
People whose browser histories would humiliate them.
People whose imaginations would horrify them if projected onto a church screen.
People who love Jesus and still find themselves fighting desires they wish had disappeared years ago.
That does not make sin harmless.
It makes grace astonishing.
Romans 5:8 says:
“While we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”
Not after you became impressive.
Not after thirty flawless days.
Not after your sexuality became perfectly ordered.
While we were still sinners.
Jesus walked knowingly toward the cross.
The nails entered His hands.
His blood was poured out.
The innocent Son of God bore the judgment sinners deserved.
And He rose from the grave.
That means your darkest sexual failure does not get the final sentence over your life.
Jesus does.
This is where repentance must be rescued from misunderstanding.
The Greek word μετάνοια — metanoia refers to repentance, a turning associated with a changed mind and direction.
Repentance is not merely feeling disgusting after orgasm.
Regret is not necessarily repentance.
Self-hatred is not repentance.
Crying is not automatically repentance.
Repentance turns.
It brings darkness into light.
It stops defending what God is exposing.
It asks what feeds the pattern.
It removes what repeatedly leads toward sin.
It seeks accountability where needed.
It learns to flee instead of negotiate.
It receives forgiveness while pursuing transformation.
Paul's instruction in 2 Timothy 2:22 is remarkably practical:
“Flee youthful passions and pursue righteousness, faith, love, and peace.”
Notice both movements.
Flee.
And...
pursue.
Christian freedom is not achieved merely by spending your entire life saying:
“Don't masturbate. Don't masturbate. Don't masturbate.”
Because a soul obsessed with avoiding darkness may still have no idea how to live in the light.
You need something greater to pursue.
Christ.
Prayer.
Friendship.
Service.
Scripture.
Meaningful work.
Healthy exercise.
Rest.
Community.
Marriage honored faithfully where applicable.
Honest conversations.
Serving hurting people.
Learning to sit before God without entertainment constantly drowning out your interior life.
You do not merely remove false comfort.
You discover a better Comforter.
Jesus said in Matthew 11:28:
“Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.”
Read those words again.
Come to Me.
That invitation reaches far beyond sexual temptation.
Come to Me when you are lonely.
Come to Me when rejection burns.
Come to Me when the memories return.
Come to Me when your body is screaming for release.
Come to Me when pornography is one tap away.
Come to Me when you have already failed.
Come to Me when you hate yourself.
Come to Me when you are tired of promising that this time will be different.
Come to Me.
Not because masturbation is somehow the greatest sin imaginable.
It isn't.
But because Christ refuses to settle for merely modifying your behavior when He intends to transform your heart.
Perhaps masturbation has become your false comfort.
Then the goal is not simply to take your comfort away.
God may be revealing the deeper hunger beneath it.
Maybe you need to grieve.
Maybe you need friendship.
Maybe you need reconciliation.
Maybe you need professional help for trauma or compulsive behavior.
Maybe you need to confess pornography use to someone trustworthy.
Maybe you need practical boundaries around your phone.
Maybe you need to stop carrying your devices into bed.
Maybe you need to recognize the emotional triggers that precede the behavior.
Maybe you need to learn that temptation often arrives when you are exhausted, isolated, angry, stressed, rejected, or bored.
And maybe you need to stop treating every relapse as proof that Christ has abandoned you.
There is an enormous difference between struggling against sin and making peace with sin.
A struggling Christian may fall.
A struggling Christian may weep.
A struggling Christian may need help repeatedly.
But there remains something inside saying:
“Jesus, I don't want anything to own the part of me that belongs to You.”
That struggle matters.
Proverbs says the righteous person falls seven times and rises again.
Your story does not have to end on the floor.
Get up.
Not because the fall was meaningless.
Not because holiness does not matter.
Get up because Christ is still worthy.
Get up because grace is not permission to remain chained; grace is God's power calling slaves into freedom.
Get up because Romans 8:1 declares:
“There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.”
And notice what Paul does not say.
He does not say there are no consequences.
He does not say there is no discipline.
He does not say Christians never struggle.
He says there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ.
The Judge became the Savior.
The debt was answered at the cross.
So when conviction comes, run toward Christ.
When condemnation whispers, “Hide from Him,” recognize the lie.
Conviction says:
“This cannot continue. Come home.”
Condemnation says:
“You are disgusting. Stay away.”
Jesus calls sinners home.
Maybe somebody reading this has never admitted the struggle to another human being.
Maybe everyone thinks you are strong.
You post Scripture.
You worship.
You serve.
You encourage other people.
And then night comes.
You know exactly what happens next.
This article is not asking you to perform public humiliation.
But it is asking you to stop pretending before God.
Tell Him the truth.
He already knows.
Tell Him what happens before the urge.
Tell Him who appears in your fantasies.
Tell Him what loneliness feels like.
Tell Him about the pornography.
Tell Him about the memories.
Tell Him about the shame afterward.
Tell Him you are tired.
Tell Him you want freedom even if part of you still wants the sin.
That last prayer may be one of the most honest prayers you ever pray:
“Jesus, part of me still wants this. But I want to want You more.”
He can work with honesty.
He already sees through performance.
And if masturbation itself is not consistently accompanied by pornography or explicit fantasy in your situation, you still have worthwhile questions to bring before God.
Does it strengthen self-control or weaken it?
Does it become compulsive?
Does it affect intimacy with your spouse?
Does it encourage fantasies about people who are not your spouse?
Does it become an escape from emotional pain?
Can you abstain freely?
Does your conscience remain troubled?
Can you sincerely bring the behavior before God and say:
“Lord Jesus, be glorified in my body”?
Romans 14 gives Christians an important principle concerning disputed matters: “Whatever does not proceed from faith is sin.”

That verse should not be ripped from context and turned into a simplistic masturbation proof-text. Paul is addressing conscience and disputable matters. But the principle remains sobering: the Christian should not deliberately bulldoze a conscience that is sincerely trying to obey God.
If you continually need to silence conviction before doing something, investigate that honestly.
And remember something else.
Not every uncomfortable feeling is automatically the Holy Spirit.
Some Christians have been taught to experience crushing shame simply for possessing sexual desire.
Sexual desire itself is not evidence that you are spiritually defective.
God created human beings as embodied, sexual creatures.
The goal is not to become incapable of desire.
The goal is for desire to come under the lordship of Jesus Christ.
That is the center of this entire conversation.
Not masturbation.
Lordship.
Who gets the throne?
Who decides what your body is for?
Who defines freedom?
Who comforts you?
Who receives your imagination?
Who teaches you what love is?
Who gets your wounds?
Who gets your loneliness?
Who gets you when nobody is watching?
Jesus did not die merely to become one more coping mechanism beside all the others.
He is Lord.
And because He is Lord, He can enter even the rooms inside you that you have kept locked for years.
That is the scandal of grace.
Christ already knows what is behind the door...
and He still knocks.
Not to humiliate you.
To redeem you.
That is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to manufacture shame.
Not to create Christians who merely look clean online.
But to keep pointing wounded, tempted, exhausted, compromised, recovering, hungry people back toward Jesus Christ, biblical truth, repentance, forgiveness, healing, discipleship, and transformation.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to tell strangers every detail.
But perhaps you need to stop fighting completely alone.
And when you see someone else write those words, don't condemn them.
Pray for them.
There is a real human being behind that comment.
Someone's son.
Someone's daughter.
Someone's husband.
Someone's wife.
Someone who may have spent years believing nobody else understands.
Let the comments become a place where grace is louder than humiliation.
Send it privately to the friend who has trusted you with their struggle.
You cannot purchase grace.
You cannot merchandise your way into forgiveness.
Jesus already paid the price you could never pay.
And perhaps tonight, when the familiar urge comes again, something will be different.
Maybe you will recognize what is underneath it.
Maybe it isn't only lust.
Maybe you are lonely.
Maybe you are hurting.
Maybe you are scared.
Maybe you are exhausted.
And instead of immediately reaching for the comfort that disappears minutes later, perhaps you will whisper:
“Jesus... I need You more than I need escape.”
Perhaps your hands will tremble.
Perhaps the temptation will not disappear instantly.
Perhaps holiness will feel less like a dramatic victory and more like surviving the next ten minutes with Christ.
Then another ten.
Then another.
And if you fall?
Do not build a house where you fell.
Confess.
Repent.
Receive His mercy.
Learn what led you there.
Reach for trustworthy help.
And rise again.
Because the Christian story was never about sinners becoming impressive enough to deserve Jesus.
It is about Jesus being powerful enough to redeem sinners.
Peter denied Him.
Thomas doubted Him.
Paul persecuted His people.
The woman caught in adultery stood publicly disgraced.
The thief beside Him was dying under judgment for his crimes.
Again and again Scripture introduces us to people whose worst chapters looked final.
Then grace entered the story.
And that may be the truth your shame desperately does not want you to believe:
The chapter you are most ashamed of may become the place where you finally discover just how far the mercy of Jesus Christ was willing to come looking for you.
